title: Water from the well
hookLine: a later story: Ananda asks an outcaste girl for water; she hesitates to give it; he says he asked for water, not her caste

cards: Ananda is thirsty, and there's a well ahead, with a young woman drawing water. He asks her for a drink. Simple enough.

Except she doesn't hand it over. She steps back and tells him what she is: a girl of the Matanga people, born outside the castes, the ones whose touch, in her world, was thought to make others unclean.
She isn't being rude. She's protecting him, by the rules she's lived under all her life. And now he has to answer.

teach.b: First, where this comes from. It's a later story, not from the Pali discourses.
It's told in Sanskrit collections like the Divyavadana and in Buddhist texts preserved in Chinese, and the tellings give the young woman a name, Prakriti. Second, her refusal.
She tells Ananda, in paraphrase: I'm a Matanga girl.
I can't give you water. She expects her birth to end the conversation. Third, his answer, the line the story is remembered for.
In paraphrase: sister, I didn't ask about your caste or your family. If you have water to spare, give it to me, and I'll drink. He doesn't give a lecture on equality.
He just won't let her birth come between a thirsty man and a cup of water. So she gives it, and he drinks.
Fourth, where the story goes next.

Later tellings carry it a long way: she falls in love with the monk who spoke to her like that, there's trouble, a spell, the Buddha steps in, and in the end she asks to join the community and becomes a nun.
The details differ from telling to telling. The heart of it doesn't. Earlier on this path the Buddha said that no one is an outcast by birth, only by what they do.

Here the same idea shows up in a cup of water. This week ran from Moggallana's powers, like the earth, two deaths, Ananda, twenty-five years and speaking for the women, to today's water from the well.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Ananda and the Matanga girl when teaching that birth and caste don't decide a person's worth, and it has been retold in later plays and dance.

games.q: you're Ananda, thirsty at a well. the young woman drawing water says she can't give it to you because of the people she was born into. what do you say?
o: thank her and look for another well.
say you asked for water, not her caste.
ask her to fetch someone else to serve you.
games.why: in paraphrase: sister, I didn't ask your caste or family. if you have water to spare, give it, and I'll drink. she gives it, and he drinks.

practice: Notice who you easily let help you and who you don't, a stranger, someone younger, someone you've decided isn't quite your kind, and see that line without judging it.
Then picture someone from the far side of it offering you something small, a seat, directions, a cup of water, and see yourself saying yes and thank you, and nothing else.
